title: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
description: Know where identity ends and permissions begin, and how ASP.NET Core enforces both.

data.text: **Question:** What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

Authentication (authn) proves **who you are** — it establishes identity from a credential. Authorization (authz) decides **what that identity is allowed to do** — it runs after authentication, per action and per resource. A user can authenticate successfully and still be forbidden from an endpoint: that is authorization doing its job.

**Authentication:**
- Verifies a credential: password, token, certificate, biometric, SSO assertion
- Runs in the authentication middleware/scheme pipeline
- Produces a `ClaimsPrincipal` — identity plus claims (name, email, provider)
- Failure means "I don't know who you are" → **401 Unauthorized**
- Can happen once (session cookie) and be reused on every request

**Authorization:**
- Evaluates rules against the established identity
- Runs in the authorization middleware and MVC filters, after authentication
- Expressed as attributes, policies, or imperative checks (`IAuthorizationService`)
- Failure means "I know who you are, but you may not do this" → **403 Forbidden**
- Is contextual: the same user may be allowed on one record and denied on another (ownership)

**How they compose in ASP.NET Core:**
- `[Authorize]` with no arguments requires any authenticated user
- Roles and claims feed into policies — authorization rules, not identity
- `[AllowAnonymous]` opts an endpoint out of the ambient authorization requirements
- Authentication schemes (cookie, JWT, API key) are pluggable; authorization rules stay the same on top of them

data.title: Identity and rules are configured separately

data.caption: Authentication establishes identity first; authorization then evaluates rules for the matched endpoint — each failure has its own status code.

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- A crisp one-line distinction, not just "authn is login"
- Knowing 401 vs 403 and when each applies
- Awareness that checks must run server-side on every request
- Understanding that authorization is contextual (roles ≠ ownership)

items: Treating a successful login as access to everything
Confusing 401 and 403, or returning 200 with an error body for both
Checking permissions only in the UI while APIs trust the client
Assuming role checks cover ownership — 'users can edit orders' vs 'users can edit THEIR orders'
Calling OAuth 2.0 an authentication protocol — it does delegated authorization; OpenID Connect adds authentication
What is the difference between 401 and 403, and what does each look like to an API client?
How do you authorize access to a specific resource a user owns?
Is OAuth 2.0 used for login? What protocol would you use instead?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Authorization runs after authentication, per endpoint and per resource
OAuth 2.0 authorizes delegated access; OpenID Connect authenticates users
data.takeaway: Identity and permissions are separate concerns — establish who the user is first, then evaluate what that user may do, on every request.
